newsitem.title: USA: River begins to recede in flooded N. Dakota city.
newsitem.headline: River begins to recede in flooded N. Dakota city.

text.p: The raging Red River receded slightly in Grand Forks on Wednesday, offering prospects of a recovery from the devastating week-long flood.

But the swollen river littered with floating telephone poles, car-sized icebergs and animal carcasses broadened its destructive path across the northern prairie into Canada, forcing thousands more people to evacuate.

"The river's receding slowly so we are in the recovery phase, which is good news," feisty Grand Forks Mayor Pat Owens said. The National Weather Service said the river level had fallen about six inches (15 centimetres) from its crest this week of just over 54 feet (16.4 metres).

Owens suggested that a few residents of a newly dry Grand Forks neighbourhood might be able to return briefly to survey the damage to their homes and she urged the city's 45,000 evacuees not to flee the city for good.
"Be upbeat, try to find something to do," she suggested. "In a week or so, we'll have more than we can handle."

Those forced to evacuate late last week after the river overwhelmed dikes protecting this city of 50,000 people have scattered to emergency shelters and homes across the state, and in some cases across the country. With fresh water from the city's still-submerged and contaminated water plant weeks away and workers struggling to maintain power and telephone service, a return to normalcy remained a dim prospect.

Many had gone days without a bath, regular hot food or any measure of privacy as they shared space with fellow evacuees. The Air Force base outside Grand Forks had temporarily run short of water and was forced to curtail showers for the 600 people still sheltering in an airplane hangar.
Several of those who tried to wait out the high water in the flood zone were being rescued after surviving even the fierce blaze that gutted sections of downtown last weekend.

Sen. Byron Dorgan, Democrat of North Dakota, said one stunned evacuee told him he had watched telephone poles, huge ice chunks and dead cows float by his window in the swift current. "It's eerie to see a city with water on the streets and no people," Dorgan said.
Further downstream toward the Canadian border, the river had spread as wide as 30 to 40 miles (48 to 64 km) across the flat plain, North Dakota's other Democratic Senator, Kent Conrad, said.
Two small North Dakota towns, Drayton and Pembina, were in a desperate race on Wednesday to build up leaking dikes as residents were told to collect crucial belongings and go.
"We're alright for now but the river is coming up," said Merl Defoe, a volunteer helping reinforce Drayton's clay, sandbag and wood barriers.

Runoff from a record winter snowpack, some of it spilling unimpeded over the landscape, covered parts of a key highway running the length of the river valley to Winnipeg, Manitoba, the next large community in the path of the floodwaters. Two Manitoba boys already have drowned in the rising floodwaters.

Canadian authorities ordered more than 17,000 people in Manitoba out of their homes and tens of thousands of head of livestock including hogs, cattle and emus were being loaded onto trucks for trips to safety.

"Because of the high temperatures of the last few days, the watershed and tributaries are flooding faster. The evacuations are taking place because the rising waters are expected to cut off access to these communities," Manitoba Emergency Management Organisation spokesman Ed Peters said.
